strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important gap: preferential BO requires rigid feedback formats, and the idea of using an LLM as a 'utility translator' between free-form natural language and GP surrogates is a sensible and well-motivated hybrid that preserves BO's uncertainty quantification and acquisition machinery.

The method is clearly specified: Algorithm 1–4 plus complete prompts (Appendix A.2) make the pipeline reproducible in principle, including details such as using 5 LLM samples per label to expose LLM uncertainty to the pairwise GP.

The empirical study is systematic: 8 environment–utility combinations with 30 replications, oracle 'gold standard' baselines (true utility BO, preferential BO), two LLM-only baselines, and informative ablations on pairwise vs. scalar utility estimation, EUBO pair selection, feedback batch size, LLM choice, and prior-knowledge types.

Useful findings beyond the headline result, e.g., that pairwise LLM labeling is more reliable than direct scalar estimation (mirroring human elicitation literature), and that EUBO-based pair selection helps the best-point-selection model even when it does not affect optimization.
The discussion honestly acknowledges limitations, including bias of LLM estimators toward their own world knowledge and the restriction of validation to LLM-simulated decision makers.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies on an LLM-simulated decision maker (Llama-3.3-70b) that is the same model as the LILO agent, and whose prompt contains a textual description of the ground-truth utility function. This creates a potential circularity: the simulated 'human' feedback is arguably optimized for an LLM to interpret, which may inflate LILO's advantage over preferential BO. No experiments with a different simulator LLM, and crucially no human study, are reported to support the claim that natural language feedback 'can be more information-rich' in realistic settings.

The claim that LILO 'substantially outperforms the true utility and preferential BO baselines' is partly an artifact of unequal feedback budgets: a single natural-language answer can convey arbitrary amounts of utility information (thresholds, relative importance, directionality), while the baselines are restricted to Bpf=2 scalars or comparisons. A fairer comparison controlling information content (e.g., longer structured descriptions in the baselines) is missing.

Internal inconsistencies undermine precision: the main text states DTLZ2 with d=4, k=8 while Appendix B.1 states d=8, k=4 (the latter consistent with the d>k constraint); Appendix A.1 contains placeholder text ('Prompts used in the LILO.xxx subroutines are presented in section A.2' alongside 'xxx subroutines').

The optimization horizon is very short (T=8) and the paper itself notes the natural-language advantage 'diminishes with increasing trials'; the reported superiority may not hold in longer, more realistic campaigns.

Robustness of the pipeline is a practical concern: the authors report they could not test models below ~14B parameters due to JSON parsing failures, suggesting fragility; no error rates on LLM labels (e.g., accuracy of LLM pairwise predictions against ground-truth preferences) are reported, which would directly quantify the quality of the 'utility translator'.

No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of an otherwise fully prompt-engineering-dependent method; also the abstract's claim of 'reliable convergence guarantees' style benefits is not backed by any theory (the paper is purely empirical).

strengths: The core idea—placing the LLM in a supporting role that translates free-form natural language feedback into GP-modelable utility signals while retaining BO's acquisition machinery—is sensible and clearly motivated; it sits in a sensible gap between rigid preferential BO and unstructured LLM optimizers.

The paper is unusually transparent about its design: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1–6), all prompts (Prompts 1–9), and explicit utility function definitions are provided, which supports reproducibility of the pipeline.

A systematic set of ablations is included: pairwise vs. scalar utility estimation, choice of pairs for LLM labeling (EUBO vs. Mx vs. random), feedback batch size, LLM model choice, feedback acquisition function for baselines, and prior-knowledge incorporation—these go beyond a single headline benchmark.

The framing of baselines (true-utility BO and preferential BO as 'gold standard' oracles; LLM 2-step and LLM direct ablations of the pipeline) is reasonable and lets the reader localize where gains come from.
The discussion section honestly identifies several limitations (LLM estimator fidelity, overly strong encoded priors, reliance on simulated decision makers) rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim rests entirely on an LLM-simulated decision maker, and in the main experiments the DM simulator and the LILO utility-estimation agent are the same model (Llama-3.3-70b-instruct). This creates a serious circularity concern: the LLM's preference labels may align with the simulated DM's answers partly because both share the same model, biases, and interpretation of the utility description, rather than because natural language feedback genuinely carries more information for real humans. No human study, no cross-model DM/agent separation as the default, and no reported accuracy of the LLM's pairwise labels against ground-truth preferences—arguably the single most important diagnostic for this method—are provided.

The headline result that LILO 'substantially outperforms the true utility BO' oracle is under-explained and likely confounded. The simulated DM is given a textual description of the global utility function and answers questions about its overall shape, so LILO effectively receives global information about g that the pairwise-comparison baseline is structurally denied. A fairer comparison would give the preferential BO baseline equivalent feedback budget or shape information; without this, the 'information-rich feedback' explanation is not well supported.

Benchmark descriptions are internally inconsistent, undermining confidence in the experiments: Section 4.1 states DTLZ2 uses d=4, k=8, while Appendix B says d=8, k=4 (and DTLZ2 requires d>k, contradicting the main-text setting); the piecewise-linear utility for Car Cab Design lists 11 entries for β1, β2, t despite k=9 outcomes; the DTLZ2 L1 optimum y_opt has 4 entries where k=8. These are exactly the details a reader needs to reproduce the benchmark.

Only T=8 iterations in low dimensions with a small set of 8 environments; error-bar conventions are inconsistent (95% CIs in Figure 3 vs. 1 standard deviation in Table 1), and many claimed improvements (e.g., Table 1 at later trials, Figure 4b right pane) are within or near the reported uncertainty, yet are described as consistent outperformance.

The claim that LILO 'has been successfully applied in multiple real-world optimization campaigns in online A/B testing' is asserted with no detail, data, or reference; as written it is an unsupported claim that should be removed or substantiated.

Numerous writing and prompt errors ('determining w whether', 'Return your final answer a a json file', 'First, analyse... then return', 'Feebdback', 'note met', 'These parameters are and their ranges are') suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread; while individually minor, their density in the method-critical prompts and setup sections erodes trust.

Cost and practicality of the method are not analyzed: each trial requires K=64 pairwise LLM labelings ×5 samples plus question generation; the DM's cognitive burden of answering 2 free-form questions per trial is claimed to be lower than pairwise comparisons but never measured, and the sample-efficiency claim ('particularly in feedback-limited regimes') is not isolated in a dedicated experiment.

No code release or repository is mentioned, and given the bespoke prompt engineering, hard-coded seeding messages, and the benchmark inconsistencies above, independent reproduction would be difficult.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical gap: combining preferential BO's principled uncertainty quantification and acquisition mechanisms with the expressive natural-language feedback interface that LLMs enable. The problem formulation (composite g∘f optimization with free-form DM feedback) is well-motivated and clearly stated.

The core design decision — placing the LLM in a supporting 'utility translator' role feeding GP surrogates rather than letting it directly propose candidates — is sensible, well-argued, and empirically supported by the LLM(2-step)/LLM(direct) ablations showing LLM-only optimizers plateau.

Systematic ablation studies: pairwise vs. scalar utility estimation, EUBO-based pair selection vs. random, prior-knowledge warm-starting (point/area/domain), feedback batch size, LLM model choice, and feedback acquisition function for baselines. These show honest scientific exploration of design choices rather than cherry-picking.

Reasonable reproducibility: full pseudocode, all prompts, test problem definitions, utility function parameters, and simulation details are provided in the appendix, allowing independent reimplementation.
The discussion includes a candid treatment of limitations (LLM estimator fidelity, potential over-encoding of model priors, no human DM evaluation yet).
weaknesses: The central evaluation is methodologically confounded: both the DM simulator and the LILO agent use the same LLM (Llama-3.3-70b) in the main experiments. The agent interpreting feedback shares biases, phrasing conventions, and world knowledge with the agent generating it, which risks circularity and could inflate LILO's apparent performance. No human study is conducted, so the claim of a 'more natural interface' for real decision makers is unverified.

The headline claim that LILO 'substantially outperforms the true utility BO' oracle baseline is not a clean comparison: the simulated DM receives pre-computed ground-truth utilities g(y_i) and a textual utility description in its prompt (Appendix B.3/Prompt 7), so its natural-language answers can leak richer functional-form information (thresholds, metric priorities) than the B_pf scalar observations or pairwise comparisons given to the baselines. The advantage may reflect an unbalanced information budget across feedback channels rather than a benefit of natural language per se. A control with information-matched feedback is needed.

Relatedly, LILO receives much denser supervision per iteration than the baselines: K=64 LLM-generated pairwise labels per trial derived from accumulated conversation history, versus B_pf=2 comparisons/scalar values for preferential/true-utility BO. The performance gap in Figure 3 is unsurprising under this asymmetry and its interpretation should be tempered.

Very short optimization horizons (T=8 iterations). The authors themselves note the advantage of natural-language feedback 'diminishes' with more trials, so claims of improved sample efficiency are demonstrated only in the regime where the effect exists.

Internal inconsistencies suggest the manuscript needs polish: Section 4.1 states DTLZ2 has d=4, k=8 while Appendix B states d=8, k=4; Section 4.1 says 'four outcome functions' while Appendix B says 'three'; Thermal Comfort Type A lists 'h_min,Tfloor = 30.0' where h_max is clearly intended; and Algorithm 2 in the appendix largely duplicates Algorithm 1 with slightly different notation (e.g., get_init_x vs. sample_init_candidates, 'Sample a batch of candidates' vs. explicit sampling).
The conclusion claims LILO 'has been successfully applied in multiple real-world optimization campaigns in online A/B testing' with no supporting details, data, or evidence anywhere in the paper.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a system whose behavior depends heavily on prompt engineering details and LLM versions.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: incorporating free-form natural language decision-maker feedback into preferential Bayesian optimization, going beyond rigid pairwise/scalar feedback formats. The design choice of placing the LLM in a 'supporting role' (feedback translation) while retaining GP-based uncertainty and principled acquisition is sensible and well-motivated.

The method is clearly presented: Algorithm 1 and 2 give a precise specification, the qEUBO-based budgeted labeling procedure is a reasonable and scalable solution to the quadratic growth of outcome pairs, and the pairwise GP formulation naturally absorbs LLM labeling noise.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: 10 environments spanning synthetic and real-world problems (DTLZ2, Vehicle Safety, Car Cab Design, Thermal Comfort, NAS-Bench-201) with multiple utility functions and personas; 16-32 replications; and extensive ablations covering feedback batch size, prior knowledge, pairwise vs. scalar estimation, labeling budget, acquisition functions, longer horizons, and alternative LLMs.

The ablations are informative: pairwise labeling beats direct scalar estimation (Fig. 6), qEUBO pair selection matters at low budgets (Fig. 7), LLM labeling accuracy (85-90%) is reported transparently (Fig. 13), and the honest long-horizon analysis (F.5) shows the NL advantage diminishes as quantitative baselines catch up. The limitation discussion is candid rather than evasive.

The demonstration on unstructured, high-dimensional outcomes (text summarization) illustrates a real capability gap relative to conventional preferential BO, which requires a surrogate over the outcome space.
weaknesses: The central evaluation rests on a simulated decision maker implemented with the same LLM (Llama-3.3-70b) as the LILO agent, and the simulator is given a textual description of the ground-truth utility function (Appendix D.3) and is instructed to 'align its preferences with the overall_utility score' (Prompt 10). This creates a potential circularity that favors LILO: the simulated DM can articulate exactly the global tradeoffs (thresholds, relative importances, shape of g) that the ground truth encodes, while the quantitative baselines receive only local, budget-limited labels. No human-subject study is conducted, so claims about 'the DM's workload' and information density of natural language remain unvalidated.

The headline claim that one natural language message 'outperforms 8-16 pairwise comparisons' (Fig. 4) depends critically on this simulator setup: the seeded DM messages directly encode properties of the utility function in natural language, effectively leaking more information than an oracle pairwise label. The paper acknowledges the comparison is 'not straightforward' but the quantitative equivalence claim is still stated strongly.

LILO beats the true-utility BO baseline, which receives actual noiseless scalar utilities - a 'gold standard'. This surprising result is explainable by the information-dense simulated messages, but it also means the main result conflates the benefit of the LILO algorithm itself with the benefit of the richer simulated feedback channel; a cleaner isolation of the algorithmic contribution is missing.

Cost accounting is incomplete: LILO uses K=64 LLM pairwise labels per trial plus question generation plus GP refits; the comparison against baselines receiving Bpf=2 human labels does not include the compute cost, prompting fragility (the authors note smaller LLMs fail with parsing errors), or sensitivity to LLM version drift.

Originality is moderate: the framework is a careful combination of existing components (Chu & Ghahramani pairwise GP, EUBO/qEUBO from Lin et al. 2022 and Astudillo et al. 2023, LLAMBO-style LLM candidate generation), with the novelty residing mainly in the language-feedback interface rather than in new methodology or theory. There is no theoretical analysis of convergence or of how LLM labeling noise affects regret.

Reproducibility is undermined by the anonymized/empty code link ('available at .' with no URL) in both the abstract and Appendix A. Prompts are provided in full, which helps, but the missing artifact release is a gap for a paper whose contribution is largely an empirical system.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: placing the LLM in a 'supporting role' (translating free-form natural-language feedback into pairwise preference labels for a pairwise GP surrogate) retains BO's calibrated uncertainty and acquisition machinery while enabling a richer feedback interface than scalar or pairwise-only preferential BO.

The method is clearly specified: Algorithm 1 and 2 give the full pipeline, including the sequential qEUBO-based pair-labeling procedure under a labeling budget, and the prompts are fully disclosed in the appendix.

The experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this line of work: 10 environments spanning synthetic and real-world problems, multiple utility function types, and extensive ablations (feedback batch size, prior knowledge, pairwise vs. scalar estimation, labeling budget K, acquisition functions, alternative LLMs, longer horizons, and unstructured text outcomes).

The paper is honest about limitations: it acknowledges the advantage of natural-language feedback diminishes over longer horizons, that smaller LLMs fail due to JSON parsing issues, that simulated DM responses were used, and that human-subject validation is future work.
A transparent 'gold standard' framing of the quantitative baselines (true utility BO and preference BO receiving noiseless feedback) makes the comparisons interpretable.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim — that natural-language feedback is more information-dense than quantitative feedback (one NL message ≈ 8-16 pairwise comparisons) — rests on a circular evaluation setup. The simulated DM agent is another LLM (Llama-3.3-70b), the same model family as the LILO agent, and is explicitly shown the ground-truth utility values of every observed outcome when generating its 'natural language' answers (Prompt 9, Appendix D.3). The 'natural-language feedback' therefore potentially encodes nearly the entire latent utility function, and its apparent information density may be an artifact of LLM-to-LLM communication rather than a property of human language feedback. This is discussed but not quantified or ablated (e.g., no experiment with degenerate/noisy DM simulations, no cross-family DM/agent pairings reported in the main results, no human study).

No human evaluation whatsoever for a paper whose entire premise is about the decision-maker's natural feedback interface. The DM's burden, question quality, and information content of real free-form feedback are all unverified; the workload-equivalence claim in Section 5.3.1 is necessarily speculative under the simulation.

The claimed 'calibrated uncertainty' of the proxy is asserted but never evaluated — there is no calibration analysis (e.g., reliability of the pairwise GP posterior under mislabeled LLM comparisons), despite calibration being one of the paper's headline selling points over LLM-only optimizers.

Methodological novelty is modest: the framework is largely a composition of existing components (Chu & Ghahramani pairwise GP, qEUBO from Astudillo et al. 2023, LogNEI, LLAMBO-style LLM candidate generation) connected by carefully engineered prompts. The primary contributions are empirical and design-level, which is acceptable, but the paper should be judged accordingly — and the evaluation does not fully support the strongest empirical claims (see circularity above).

The advantage over quantitative baselines shrinks and can reverse at longer horizons (Appendix F.5), and the main experiments use only T = 8 batched trials, so the practical regime where LILO wins appears narrow; the reported superiority in 'feedback-limited regimes' is precisely the regime most sensitive to the simulated-DM design choice.

The unstructured-outcomes experiment (summarization) is small (d = 4, T = 5 trials) and the DM simulator there is again given the oracle utility indicators, weakening the demonstration that LILO 'recovers' preference information from language.
Reproducibility is claimed but the code link is empty in the manuscript; results depend on nontrivial prompt engineering and an external LLM API, which limits independent verification.

strengths: The problem setting is well motivated: preferential BO with rich, free-form natural language feedback is a natural gap between rigid pairwise-feedback methods and LLM-as-optimizer approaches, and the 'LLM in a supporting role' design (LLM labels preferences, GP surrogate + standard acquisition drives optimization) is a sensible and clearly articulated architecture that preserves calibrated uncertainty.

The empirical study is unusually thorough: 10 environments spanning synthetic and real-world problems (including NAS-Bench-201 and a summarization setting with unstructured outcomes), 16–32 replications, and extensive ablations covering feedback batch size, prior-knowledge types, pairwise vs. scalar labeling, qEUBO vs. random pair selection under labeling budgets, acquisition functions, LLM choice, and longer horizons.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly reports that LILO's advantage diminishes at longer horizons and that quantitative baselines eventually catch up, that simulated DM responses were used for controlled evaluation, and it discusses the dependence on LLM interpretation of nuanced feedback in the discussion section.

Practical design choices are studied rather than asserted: the sequential qEUBO-based labeling procedure (Algorithm 2) is justified by an ablation (Fig. 7), pairwise labeling is shown to beat direct scalar LLM utility estimates (Fig. 6), and the pairwise-label accuracy analysis (Fig. 13, 85–90%) supports the feasibility of the LLM labeling step.
Reproducibility support is good in spirit: all prompts are provided verbatim, baseline algorithms are fully specified in pseudocode, and code for reproducing results is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies on an LLM-simulated decision maker (Llama-3.3-70b) that is given a textual description of the ground-truth utility. Since both the feedback simulator and the LILO labeling agent are LLMs, the headline claim that 'one natural language message outperforms 8–16 pairwise comparisons or ground-truth utility evaluations' may be substantially an artifact of simulator–agent compatibility: the simulated DM can articulate thresholds and trade-offs in text form that the same-family LLM interprets easily, which may not reflect real human feedback quality or information density. No human-subject study is included, so the key claim about real decision makers is essentially untested.

The result that LILO outperforms even the noiseless true-utility BO 'gold standard' baseline is surprising and, given the simulator setup above, likely reflects information leakage through the simulated feedback rather than a genuine advantage over directly observed utilities; the paper's explanation (language conveys 'richer information') is plausible but not disentangled from the simulation design.

There is no theoretical component: the BO machinery (pairwise GP, Laplace approximation, EUBO/qEUBO, LogNEI) is entirely standard, and the contribution is primarily a prompting-and-plumbing system. This is acceptable for a framework paper, but the novelty over prior LLM+BO hybrids (e.g., LLAMBO, LLM-based preference elicitation) is incremental — mainly the free-form-feedback-as-labels interface.

The comparison of DM workload between Bpf=1 natural language messages and Bpf=16 pairwise comparisons is acknowledged as 'not straightforward', yet Figure 4's headline equivalence claim rests on this unvalidated analogy; the questions LILO asks are also auto-generated, which may elicit more structured answers than a human would spontaneously provide.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on a specific LLM (the authors note smaller models fail with JSON parsing errors) and by the anonymized/blank code URL in the manuscript ('available at .'); results for LLM-driven pipelines are inherently sensitive to model version, which is only partially addressed by the F.7 ablation.

The summarization experiment (Fig. 8/17) shows LILO only 'matches' the strongest baselines with maximum oracle feedback, and the benchmark is small (T=5 trials, 4 decoding parameters), so the claim of compatibility with unstructured outcomes is illustrated rather than convincingly established.
